// dryRunTimeoutMinutes: Stryker runs the whole suite once, instrumented, before it throws a single mutant, and its default ceiling for that is FIVE MINUTES. Measured 2026-09-14 on an idle 8-core machine: 1266 tests in 4 minutes and 57 seconds. Three seconds of margin is not a margin — the run had already failed twice here and the nightly had been red for two days, each time with `Initial test run timed out` and no report to read. This number is a CEILING and not a budget: what it guards against is a runner that has hung, and that does not care whether the value is 12 or 20, while a runner with half these cores does. It is declared rather than defaulted so that the reason stands beside it, and point 1 of `check-mutation` refuses the default.
// concurrency: Stryker derives its default from the core count, and on this eight-core machine that default takes the PARENT process with it — no red, no report, no session to read one in (`lesson-200`). The binding resource is not cores but memory per worker: each one runs a full Vitest process over the instrumented sandbox, and that is nearly the same on both machines this ever runs on — 15 GB here, 16 GB on `ubuntu-latest`. So one number is right in both places although the core counts are eight and four, which is what lets it live here instead of on a command line, where it was correct on one machine and absent everywhere else. It is a CEILING on memory and not a knob for speed: raising it on a larger machine is precisely how the parent process dies. Point 1 of `check-mutation` refuses its absence AND a command line that overrides it, because an override is the same fact in a second place.
// mutate:
The denominator of the measurement, and `mutation.policy.json` holds a copy of it so that changing it is a comparison rather than an act of trust. Two entries here are decisions and not shorthand.

FIRST, `schematics/migrations/**` is IN and `schematics/ng-add/**` is out. The two run in the same place and are measured in different ones: `ng add` is executed by `check-consumer`, which installs the package into a real application and runs it there, while NO gate in this workspace executes a migration — its spec is the only instrument it has, and a spec nothing measures is a spec whose gaps nobody can see. Three separate reviews of the first migration each found survivors by planting mutants BY HAND, which is the same measurement done by an eye that gets tired. Measured on this desk, four workers, with no stray job holding a core: the file is 280 mutants and 143 seconds of wall clock run on its own, of which six are its own initial run and some twenty are Stryker starting — so about TWO MINUTES of mutants, for 5.2% more of them (5426 to 5706). The clause is narrow on purpose, because it is all that was checked: the same measurement read 159 seconds while a stray process of this work's own making held a core for a day, and the desk is shared, so `nproc` and a load average would say more than this does (`lesson-239`). It was 467 mutants and 249 seconds while the migration read `.html` with a scan of its own — that one taken inside the window above and never repeated, so it is an upper bound and the two readings do not share a machine condition. What the change did to the file is better counted than timed: 232 lines of code became 197, and every timeout left with them (`lesson-236`). The whole run came to 78 minutes and that reading is an UPPER BOUND, taken while that same core was gone; the marginal number is the one to read anyway, because the total moves with the machine and this file's share of it does not. A separate target was the alternative and costs the same compute, because `vitest.related` already scopes the initial run to the specs of whatever is mutated (measured on this tree: the glob as it stood before this entry executes 1274 of the suite's 1425 tests, and the 151 it leaves out are exactly this spec; an initial run over the schematics alone executes that spec and nothing else) — what it cannot do is satisfy point 3 of `check-mutation`, which asks whether the specs of the library ran in THIS report. Before this entry the answer for the migration's spec was no, and `coversNothing` is empty.

SECOND, the barrel exclusion names `*/src/index.ts` and not `**/index.ts`. Counted 2026-09-21: the library holds 37 files called `index.ts`, of which 34 are an entrypoint's `src/index.ts` and are re-export barrels. The other three are NOT. Two are the schematics factories, named that because the Angular CLI resolves a factory by the path it is given (`./migrations/badge-tone/index#badgeTone`), and they carry the whole of what they do. The third, `libs/components/src/index.ts`, IS a barrel — and it needs no exclusion here, because no include above reaches `libs/components/src/**`. `check-mutation` excuses it separately and has to: its candidate set is the whole git index under the library rather than this glob, so it asks `endsWith('/src/index.ts')` and covers all 35. The wider spelling struck the migration out of the measurement while reading like a rule about barrels, which is the quietest way for a file to leave a denominator (`lesson-45`).
// ignorePatterns: Stryker copies the repository into a sandbox and walks it ITSELF, not the git index: without this list it saw 3907 files where git knows 708. The excess is generated directories, and those have concurrent writers — `nx affected` runs `build` beside `mutation`, ng-packagr creates and deletes `tmp/libs/components/build/tsconfig.generated.<uuid>.json`, and Stryker falls over on `ENOENT ... copyfile` halfway through copying. The symptom is misleading at that: the task is flaky and passes on its own, so the first suspect was the mutant timeout. In passing, the sandbox stops copying its own previous sandboxes from `tmp/stryker`. The agent directories are here for a second reason and not for their size: two of them hold SYMLINKS to a tree in a third, and `copyFile` on a link to a directory is `EISDIR` — the run ends before the first mutant. Taking those trees out of the git index did not help and could not, because Stryker walks the WORKING TREE: what git no longer tracks is still on disk, and this list is the only place that can say so.
